Sabbath Year
SAB-uth yeer
noun phrase (biblical institution)
From Hebrew shemittah ("release, letting drop") and shabbath ("rest, cessation"). The sabbatical year, every seventh year, in which the land rested, debts were released, and the poor were provided for (Exod 23; Lev 25; Deut 15).

📖 Biblical Definition

The Sabbath year (or sabbatical year, Hebrew shemittah) was the seventh year in Israel's God-appointed calendar, a year of rest and release patterned on the weekly Sabbath: just as the seventh day was holy rest, so the seventh year was a year of rest for the land, release for debtors, and provision for the poor. Three main provisions are given. First, the land rested: the fields were not sown nor the vineyards pruned, and whatever grew of itself was left for the poor, the stranger, and even the beasts (Exod 23:10-11; Lev 25:1-7). This taught Israel that the land was the LORD's and that the people lived by His provision, not merely by their own labor — and it gave the soil its rest. Second, debts were released: at the end of every seven years, the creditor released what his fellow Israelite owed him (Deut 15:1-11), so that poverty would not become permanent bondage. Third, Hebrew bondservants were released in the seventh year of their service (Exod 21:2; Deut 15:12-18), sent away not empty but furnished liberally from the master's flock and floor. The Sabbath year embodied the LORD's care for the land, the poor, the debtor, and the servant, and it tested Israel's faith: would they trust God to provide in the year they did not sow? The repeated failure of Israel to keep the Sabbath years is given by the Chronicler as a reason for the seventy-year exile — the land would have its sabbaths while the people were away (2 Chr 36:21; cf. Lev 26:34-35). The institution looks forward to the rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9) and to the Jubilee, the sabbath of sabbatical years.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The seventh year (Hebrew shemittah) of rest and release: the land rested, debts were released, and Hebrew bondservants were freed (Exod 23; Lev 25; Deut 15); taught that the land is the LORD's and tested Israel's trust in His provision.

SABBATH YEAR, noun phrase. Hebrew shemittah ("release"); the seventh, sabbatical year of rest and release.

The land rested (no sowing or pruning; the self-grown left for the poor and the beasts) — Exod 23:10-11; Lev 25:1-7.

Debts were released among Israelites at the end of every seven years (Deut 15:1-11).

Hebrew bondservants were freed in the seventh year of service, furnished liberally (Exod 21:2; Deut 15:12-18).

Israel's failure to keep the Sabbath years is given as a reason for the 70-year exile (2 Chr 36:21); points to the rest that remains (Heb 4:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 25:3-4 — "Six years thou shalt sow thy field, and six years thou shalt prune thy vineyard, and gather in the fruit thereof; But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD."

Deuteronomy 15:1-2 — "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release. And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother."

2 Chronicles 36:21 — "To fulfil the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths: for as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath, to fulfil threescore and ten years."

Hebrews 4:9 — "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Sabbath year is corrupted when read as mere agricultural pragmatism (crop rotation) rather than a faith-testing act of worship, when its provision for the poor and the debtor is ignored, or when its testimony to the land as the LORD's is reduced to economics.

expand to see more

Agricultural-pragmatism reduction. Modern readers sometimes explain the Sabbath year as ancient agronomy — a sensible crop-rotation policy to let the soil recover. While the land did benefit, the institution's stated ground is theological, not agronomic: the seventh year is "a sabbath for the LORD" (Lev 25:4), a year of worshipful trust in which Israel did not sow and yet expected God to provide (Lev 25:20-22 promises a triple harvest in the sixth year). The Sabbath year was an act of faith and worship that tested whether Israel believed the land was the LORD's and the people lived by His provision. To reduce it to crop rotation is to miss the worship at its heart.

Mercy-provisions ignored. The Sabbath year's provisions for the poor, the debtor, and the servant are sometimes overlooked in favor of the land-rest alone. Yet the release of debts (Deut 15) and the freeing of bondservants (Deut 15:12-18) are central: the institution exists so that poverty among God's people would not harden into permanent bondage, and so that the servant would go free furnished, not empty. The Sabbath year embodies the LORD's care for the vulnerable — the same care that runs through the gleaning laws, the Jubilee, and the whole Mosaic provision for the poor. It is mercy structured into the calendar.
